description: Prince and the Revolution's soaring second single from Parade, the soundtrack to Under the Cherry Moon. Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman wrote the music, Prince added the lyrics, and the horns do the rest.

pops.text: Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman composed the music in London while Prince was in France filming Under the Cherry Moon. He added the lyrics later back in Minneapolis.
Basic tracking happened on 30 November 1985 at the Washington Avenue Warehouse in Minneapolis, according to Prince Vault. A full-band day for a mostly solo-minded album.
Prince initially claimed sole credit for the song on release, Prince Vault notes. The published writing credit now names Prince with Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman on music.
This was the earliest released Prince recording to feature trumpeter Atlanta Bliss. His horn partner here is saxophonist Eric Leeds, and together they punch up the whole track.
The album version runs 3:58 and segues straight into 'Do U Lie?' on Parade. The 12-inch extended version stretches the groove out to 10:03.
It reached No. 23 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the US but only No. 45 in the UK. A towering single that somehow stayed a cult favorite.
The B-side was the instrumental 'Alexa de Paris,' one of the few Parade-era tracks built around a guitar solo. Parade famously has almost no electric lead guitar on the album itself.
Both songs appear in Under the Cherry Moon, with 'Mountains' playing as the credits roll. The film is black-and-white, but the MTV version of the video was shown in color.
The official video was directed by Prince himself and released in April 1986. Yes, even the visuals were in-house.
Parade was Prince's eighth album, released 31 March 1986, and 'Mountains' was its second single, out about six weeks later. It still sounds like the Revolution at full strength.

title: Mountains

description: The Banshees' gloriously backwards lead single from Peepshow, built on a reversed brass loop. It became their first US chart single and the first-ever No. 1 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart.

pops.text: That woozy sound is real tape trickery: the song was built on a loop played in reverse of a brass part the band had arranged in 1987 for a cover of John Cale's 'Gun.'
The band picked favorite bits of that backwards tape, edited them, and re-recorded on top, adding accordion, a one-note bass and jarring guitar. Drummer Budgie then added another beat.
Siouxsie sang her vocal over the finished backwards backing, and used a different microphone for each line. It took the band about a year to arrive at the final result.
Released 18 July 1988 as the first single from Peepshow, the band's ninth studio album. Peepshow followed in September 1988.
In September 1988 Billboard launched its Modern Rock Tracks chart, and 'Peek-a-Boo' was the chart's first No. 1 song. Alternative radio literally starts its chart era here.
It was also the Banshees' first single to reach the Billboard Hot 100, peaking at No. 53 in December 1988. In the UK it peaked at No. 16, their fifth Top 20 hit.
Melody Maker called it '1930s hip hop,' while the NME went with 'Oriental marching band hip hop.' Critics were reaching for comparisons because nothing else sounded like it.
The chorus lines about 'jeepers' and 'peepers' were judged too close to the 1938 standard 'Jeepers Creepers.' The band gave co-writing credit to Harry Warren and Johnny Mercer to settle it.
Sir Mix-a-Lot sampled it the next year on 'The (Peek-a-Boo) Game' from his 1989 album Seminar. From goth clubs to rap records in twelve months.
The video was later watched and commented on by Beavis and Butt-Head, and the song arrived as downloadable content for Rock Band on 20 April 2010. Peek-a-boo, indeed.

title: Peek-A-Boo

description: Siouxsie and the Banshees' shimmering dance-pop tribute to Jayne Mansfield, and their biggest US hit. Producer Stephen Hague, tabla player Talvin Singh and a borrowed hip-hop beat helped it top the alternative chart.

pops.text: Siouxsie's cryptic lyrics are an ode to actress Jayne Mansfield. Her catchword 'divoon,' her heart-shaped swimming pool and her love of champagne and parties all turn up in the song.
The title itself is borrowed: Kiss Them for Me was a 1957 film starring Mansfield opposite Cary Grant. Old Hollywood glamour, Banshees style.
The darker turn in the lyric points to the 1967 car crash that killed Mansfield. It is a party song with a tragedy quietly running underneath it.

Producer Stephen Hague, known for work with Pet Shop Boys and New Order, gave the band a more straightforward pop sound than their post-punk and goth records. Superstition was recorded at RAK Studios in London.
Twenty-year-old tabla player Talvin Singh played on the sessions and sang during the bridge. It was the first of his many collaborations with pop artists, before his work with Björk.
The drum beat came from a Roland TR-909 pattern previously used on Schoolly D's 1985 single 'P.S.K. What Does It Mean?' A hip-hop foundation under a Banshees single.
Released 13 May 1991 as the first single from Superstition, the band's tenth studio album. The album followed on 10 June 1991.
It became the band's biggest US hit, peaking at No. 23 on the Billboard Hot 100, and spent five weeks at No. 1 on Modern Rock Tracks in July and August 1991. In the UK it reached No. 32.

The 'Snapper Mix' adds a spoken sample of Mansfield herself from Will Success Spoil Rock Hunter?, while the 'Kathak Mix' by Youth opens with samples of Robert Anton Wilson. Remix culture, 1991 edition.
School of Seven Bells covered the song in 2010, nearly two decades later. Mansfield's pink champagne kept bubbling.

title: Kiss Them For Me

description: An uplifting instrumental standout from STS9's 2016 album The Universe Inside, released on their own 1320 Records. The band says it is about people's power to change the world — as a promise and as a warning.

pops.text: STS9 stands for Sound Tribe Sector 9. The instrumental band formed in Georgia in 1998 and later relocated to Northern California, building everything around live performance.
'World Go Round' was debuted live on 28 March 2014 at the McDowell Mountain Music Festival in Phoenix. That was STS9's first show back after cancelling their winter tour.
That Phoenix show was also the band's first with bassist Alana Rocklin, following founding bassist David Murphy's departure earlier in 2014. A new era started with new songs.
The studio version arrived on The Universe Inside, released in 2016 on the band's own label, 1320 Records. STS9 founded 1320 to release their own music independently.

In the official audio description, the band says the song 'speaks to the fact that people have the power to change the world.' They call it uplifting, but also a warning if that power is not used for good.

The Universe Inside was a vocal-forward step for a mostly instrumental band, with singer Maureen Murphy guesting on several album tracks live and in the studio era. 'World Go Round' itself lets the instruments carry the message.

Two nights after its debut, the song got only its second-ever performance on 12 April 2014 in Vail, Colorado, on a night the band also revived 'Poseidon' for the first time since 2004. Collectors noticed.
At Red Rocks on 9 September 2016, 'World Go Round' closed the second set of STS9's 20th performance at the famous amphitheatre. New album, landmark venue, set closer.
The band spelled out a joke with it on Halloween 2015 in Maryland, using song titles to spell 'Happy Halloween D.C.' 'World Go Round' appeared as a second encore that night.
STS9 describe their sound as post-rock dance music, mixing live instruments with electronics, funk, jazz and hip-hop influences. This track's steady build is that formula in miniature.

title: World Go Round

description: A blissful instrumental from STS9's 2011 EP When the Dust Settles, named for San Francisco's famous bridge. A Bay Area favorite ever since, it is a staple of the band's live sets and acoustic reinventions.

pops.text: 'Golden Gate' was released on 7 June 2011 by 1320 Records as part of the When the Dust Settles EP. The studio version runs 5:12.

It is named after San Francisco's iconic Golden Gate Bridge, and live reviews have long noted how fitting it feels when STS9 play it for Bay Area crowds. The band relocated to Northern California in 2000.
When the Dust Settles also gave fans 'Scheme' and the title track, and the EP is still counted among the band's best-loved short releases. 'Golden Gate' sits right in its heart.
STS9 formed in Georgia in 1998 as Sound Tribe Sector 9, a name referencing the Mayan calendar. They built their following almost entirely through relentless touring and festival sets.
The band releases music on their own 1320 Records, founded in 2005. Independence is not a footnote for STS9 — it is the business model.

In November 2011 at Athens' Georgia Theatre, the band celebrated the venue's return after fire damage by dressing as firemen and opening to Talking Heads' 'Burning Down the House.' 'Golden Gate' featured in the first set that night.
PopMatters, reviewing the band's April 2012 Oakland shows, called 'Golden Gate' a gem from the EP that 'really comes alive onstage,' carried by a blissful collective groove. Bay Area home game, won.
On 27 August 2016 in Alpharetta, Georgia, 'Golden Gate' opened STS9's all-acoustic 'Axe the Cables' set — the first time the song had been played that way. Same tune, no cables.
It opened for a famous pairing on New Year's Eve 2018 in Denver too, sitting in a first-set run that included 'Menacer' before it. A trusted utility player in big-night setlists.
The official video here is STS9's own live performance at Red Rocks in 2021, the Colorado amphitheatre the band had already played more than twenty times by 2016. Some songs are built to travel.

title: Golden Gate

description: Kevin Parker's stomping glam-psych broadside at the swaggering 'jock,' rescued from the vault to become the lead single from Lonerism (2012) — and Tame Impala's unlikely breakthrough.

pops.text: Old song alert! Parker told Stereogum in 2012 that 'Elephant' was one of his oldest songs — it sat in the vaults for years before a soundcheck run-through rescued it.
First out of the gate: 'Elephant' arrived in July 2012 as the lead single from the second Tame Impala album, Lonerism, the follow-up to 2010's Innerspeaker.
It's not about a loner — it's about the bully. Parker told NME the song skewers 'the jock, the guy who thinks he's great,' seen through a bitter recluse's eyes.
Tame Impala is basically a one-man studio: on record, Kevin Parker writes, plays and produces everything himself. The full band only assembles for live shows.
That melty, strobing video? It was directed by Japanese-born New York multimedia artist Yoshi Sodeoka, a pioneer of glitchy analog-meets-digital visuals.
Australia voted early: 'Elephant' stomped to No. 7 in Triple J's Hottest 100 for 2012, with 'Feels Like We Only Go Backwards' close behind at No. 9.
Phone ad fame: the song's stomping riff was licensed for advertisements for the BlackBerry Z10, taking Parker's psych-rock to prime-time TV.
Near miss! Parker later told Zane Lowe that 'Elephant' almost didn't make Lonerism at all — it scraped onto the album and became its signature song.
Bittersweet royalty check: Parker admitted he was a little embarrassed by the song's swagger, noting it 'paid for half my house.'
Full-circle moment: in 2021 The Wiggles covered 'Elephant' for Triple J's Like a Version — and it topped the Hottest 100, the first cover ever to win the countdown.

title: Elephant

description: After four silent years, Kevin Parker returned in 2019 with a piano-led swirl of '70s disco and '90s house about time slipping by — a standalone single that never made The Slow Rush.

pops.text: The comeback: released on 22 March 2019, 'Patience' was the first new Tame Impala music since the Grammy-nominated album Currents back in 2015.
No long tease campaign here — Parker announced it on Instagram with about an hour's notice: 'New track. 1 hour. Speakers/headphones ready people.'
Recipe card: the official press release pitched it as a mid-tempo chugger mixing 1970s disco and 1990s house, 'stoned on the house-made Tame Impala lysergic liquor.'
One-man band, again: Parker wrote, produced, sang and played everything on 'Patience.' The only other credit is Dave Cooley, who mastered it.
Spot it if you can: the word 'patience' never actually appears anywhere in the song's lyrics. The title is the whole mood, not a hook.
The song is a meditation on life's cycles and phases — Parker making peace with the passing of time as the seasons change and his days stay 'shapeless.'
TV debut: on 30 March 2019 Tame Impala made their Saturday Night Live debut, hosted by Sandra Oh, playing 'Patience' and unveiling a brand-new song, 'Borderline.'
Album? What album? Despite launching the new era, 'Patience' was left off the standard edition of the next album, The Slow Rush, in 2020.
Collectors' consolation: 'Patience' later surfaced on the Japanese edition of The Slow Rush and in its 2022 deluxe box set, remixes included.
Industry nod: at the 2019 ARIA Awards, Parker was nominated for both Producer of the Year and Engineer of the Year for his work on this one track.

title: Patience

description: Sting's post-apocalyptic shrug from Zenyatta Mondatta (1980): one hypnotic three-chord loop, an old VCR, a James Brown tape and an Otis Redding record — everything that's still around.

pops.text: Track three on Zenyatta Mondatta, the Police's third album, released in October 1980 — and yes, that whole sentence really is the song's title.
Sting calls it a post-apocalyptic vision: he imagined himself the sole survivor of a holocaust, with all his favourite things still intact around him.
Minimalism as a feature: the song repeats the same three-chord progression for its entire 3 minutes 38 seconds, building a hypnotic, dance-rock loop.
Survivor's inventory, per the lyrics: the same VCR he's had for years, James Brown on the T.A.M.I. Show, one Otis Redding song — 'it's all I own.'
Rush job: Zenyatta Mondatta was written on tour and recorded in just four weeks at Wisseloord Studios in Hilversum, Netherlands, in the summer of 1980.
Stewart Copeland's diary entry from hell: 'We finished the album at 4 a.m. on the day we were starting our next world tour' — then drove to Belgium for the first gig.
Why Holland? Tax reasons kept the band from recording in Britain, so they took Surrey Sound producer Nigel Gray with them to Wisseloord instead.
Disco Police: paired with 'Voices Inside My Head,' this song reached No. 3 on Billboard's Disco Top 100 chart in early 1981.
Sting kept it for himself: on his solo live album Bring on the Night, he performs it as a medley with the earlier Police song 'Bring on the Night.'
Remix afterlife: in 2000, Different Gear vs. the Police reworked it as 'When the World Is Running Down (You Can't Go Wrong)' — a UK No. 28 and US dance-chart No. 7 hit.

title: When The World Is Running Down, You Make The Best Of What's Still Around

description: The opening shot of Ghost in the Machine (1981), written by Sting on a Casio keyboard in the back of a truck — a ska-tinged, synth-led hit about souls trapped in a material world.

pops.text: Opening track, opening statement: 'Spirits' kicks off the Police's fourth album, Ghost in the Machine, released on 2 October 1981.
Written in transit: Sting composed it on a little Casio keyboard while riding in the back of a truck. 'I just tap, tap, tap and there it was, just by accident.'
That Casio was a Casiotone M10, and its preset pattern did the heavy lifting — Stewart Copeland has joked it was 'in a way, the first song written by AI.'
Heavy reading: the song and the album title both draw on Hungarian philosopher Arthur Koestler, whose book The Ghost in the Machine Sting admired.
Band argument No. 4,081: Sting wanted to record it with no guitar at all. Andy Summers fought back, and they compromised — both play the riff, with the synth turned up over the guitar.
Recorded at AIR Studios on the Caribbean island of Montserrat, with Hugh Padgham producing — a far cry from a truck cab.
Drummer's nightmare: Copeland calls this his hardest Police song to play — the syncopated beat keeps dodging the downbeat. 'Pat your head, rub your tummy' territory.
Chart spirits: released as a single in December 1981, it reached No. 12 in the UK and No. 11 in the US in early 1982.
Key change on stage: live, the band played the song in D minor, even though the studio version is in A minor.
Reggae revival: in 1995 Pato Banton covered it as a duet with Sting for the Ace Ventura: When Nature Calls soundtrack, reaching No. 36 in the UK.

title: Spirits In The Material World

description: An obscure 2010 deep-funk workout from the Underbelly with singer Roxie Ray, issued by Milan's Record Kicks label on its SoulShaker Vol. 7 compilation — no video, just groove.

pops.text: Deep cut of deep cuts: this funk workout first appeared in 2010 on Record Kicks, the Milan-based label specialising in modern funk and soul.
Compilation fame: 'Shepard's Pie' was track 4 on SoulShaker Vol. 7, Record Kicks' showcase compilation — which is why the label's own YouTube upload titles it '04.'
Clock check: the track runs 3 minutes 59 seconds — a tight, DJ-friendly single length, built for the dancefloor rather than the album sprawl.
Spelling bee fail: the label's upload calls it 'shepards pie' with no apostrophe, while streaming services list it as 'shepard's pie.' Neither spells it 'shepherd's.'
The voice out front is Roxie Ray's — she also recorded with funk outfit Dojo Cuts, fellow travellers in the same modern deep-funk scene.
House band energy: Shazam lists this among the Underbelly's top tracks, alongside fellow Roxie Ray features 'Funky Retro,' 'Eric FM' and 'V Funk.'
BBC-approved funk: the band's Roxie Ray tracks earned live sessions on BBC 6 Music, including Craig Charles's Funk and Soul Show — the UK's funk tastemaker slot.
No video, no problem: there is no music video for this song. The uploads are official audio only — this Topic-channel version and the Record Kicks label catalogue post.
Second life on the lino: breakdancers adopted the track — YouTube is full of uploads presenting 'Shepard's Pie' specifically as b-boy battle music.
Still underground: its afterlife ran through funk DJs and breakdance battles rather than the charts — a cult groove that dancers kept passing around.

title: Shepard's Pie

description: The closing track of Seven Feet Under, the 2010 debut album by Cornwall funk five-piece The Underbelly, with Dojo Cuts singer Roxie Ray on vocals — a deep-funk groove on Milan's Record Kicks label.

pops.text: Last song, last word: 'Funky Retro' closes Seven Feet Under — it is track 13 of 13 on The Underbelly's debut album.
The album arrived on March 22, 2010, on Record Kicks — a label based in Milan, Italy, founded in 2003 and devoted to deep funk, soul and Afrobeat.
The Underbelly are a five-piece from Cornwall, England: tenor and alto sax, flute and baritone sax, guitar, bass and drums. That is a lot of horns for one band.
The voice belongs to Roxie Ray, who came to the band from Australia's Dojo Cuts — whose own album on Record Kicks had landed a year earlier, in 2009.
Settle in: at 4 minutes 36 seconds, this is no quickie single edit. It is a full album groove, built to stretch out and work the dancefloor.
Before the album, the band made a big splash at the UK's legendary Jelly Jazz parties, championed by DJs including Eddie Pillar and Diesler, per the label's own sales notes.
They were BBC 6 Music favorites, too: The Underbelly recorded live sessions for The Craig Charles Funk & Soul Show, including 'I Keep Heading On' with Roxie Ray singing.
That tune, 'I Keep Heading On,' was the album's advance single — backed with a B-side called 'Cold Toast.' Breakfast, but make it funk.
Catalog collectors, take note: Seven Feet Under is Record Kicks RKX 030, issued on both vinyl LP and CD in 2010.
Roxie Ray later recorded under the name Sarsha Simone — MusicBrainz lists Roxie Ray as her alias. The funk stayed; only the name changed.

title: Funky Retro

description: The opening track of Damn the Torpedoes, co-written by Mike Campbell and Tom Petty and recorded, by Campbell's count, around 100 times. A defiant rocker from the band's breakthrough album.

pops.text: Mike Campbell wrote the music — one of the first songs he ever wrote — and handed it to Tom Petty, who put the words over it exactly as it was, no changes.
Campbell's trick in the chorus: it lifts up and soars without changing chords. Petty found the way to make it rise while the band stays put.
It started as a 4-track demo Campbell made at his house. Getting the band version to feel right in the studio was another matter entirely.
Campbell told Songfacts: 'We must have recorded that 100 times.' At one point he got so frustrated he left the studio and went out of town for two days — the only time he ever did that.

It opens Damn the Torpedoes, an album Petty recorded while fighting his record company over his contract — a dispute in which he declared bankruptcy before MCA renegotiated and launched the Backstreet label for it.
The album spent seven weeks at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, kept out of No. 1 by Pink Floyd's The Wall. It later went triple platinum in the US.
Released as a single on January 11, 1980, with 'It's Rainin' Again' on the B-side. At 3:25, it is all muscle — no wasted motion.
Chart report: No. 15 on the Billboard Hot 100, but No. 2 in Canada and No. 3 in New Zealand. The rest of the world heard it even louder.
Listen for the shaker — that is session great Jim Keltner, of all people, on samba shaker. Cash Box praised the 'growing interplay between guitar and organ' behind Petty's vocal.
Rolling Stone ranked it No. 2 on its 2020 list of the 50 greatest Tom Petty songs. Melissa Etheridge covered it in 2005 — and so, believe it or not, did Alvin and the Chipmunks.

title: Refugee

description: Tom Petty's first Top 10 hit began as a 1974 Mudcrutch demo he nearly gave to the J. Geils Band. Producer Jimmy Iovine rescued it for Damn the Torpedoes — and it launched the breakthrough.

pops.text: Old song, new band: Petty wrote this in 1974 and first demoed it with Mudcrutch, his pre-Heartbreakers band — five years before it became a hit.
He dreamed it up while driving, then booked a studio by himself for an hour, banged it out on the piano, and went home. Songwriting, express lane.

Petty nearly gave it away to the J. Geils Band, whose sound he thought it fit. Singer Peter Wolf later said Petty sent it on tape in 1977 — while the band was busy mixing an album, and it went unused.

It nearly missed the album, too. Petty recalled that assistant engineer Tory Swinson, asleep on the control-room sofa, raised his head and said, 'What about that Don't Do Me Like That? I really like that one.'
Producer Jimmy Iovine convinced Petty to keep it for Damn the Torpedoes, sensing a hit. Iovine's instincts: correct.
It was the album's lead single, released November 5, 1979, with 'Casa Dega' on the US B-side and 'Century City' on the UK one.
No fat on this one: the whole song clocks in at just 2:44. Record World called its hook 'irresistible,' and the Fort Worth Star-Telegram ranked it the fourth-best single of 1979.
It peaked at No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 — Petty's first Top 10 — and remains the Heartbreakers' only solo song ever to crack the Top 10. In Canada it went all the way to No. 3.
Britain shrugged: despite airplay on London's Capital Radio in the summer of 1980, the single failed to make the UK Top 75 at all.
That 1974 Mudcrutch version finally surfaced in the mid-1990s on Playback, Petty's career-spanning box set — the demo that almost got given away, kept after all.

title: Don't Do Me Like That

description: The Joshua Tree's opening track: The Edge's delay-drenched arpeggio, Bono's Belfast-inspired lyric, and a rooftop video that shut down downtown Los Angeles and won a Grammy.

pops.text: The Edge composed the music in one night at his new home, Melbeach House, on a four-track — setting out to conjure 'the ultimate U2 live song.' With nobody home to hear it, he danced around punching the air.

Bono's lyric answers a story from Belfast, where your religion and income could be read from the street you lived on. He contrasted it with the anonymity he felt in Ethiopia — and first wrote the words on an airsickness bag there.

Recording it nearly broke the band. With its time-signature shifts and constant chord changes, co-producer Daniel Lanois called it 'the science project song' and walked them through it with a schoolhouse blackboard and pointer.

Brian Eno estimated half of The Joshua Tree sessions went to this one song — and he planned to erase the tapes so they'd start fresh. Engineer Pat McCarthy walked in, dropped his tea tray, and physically restrained him.
The finished studio version is compiled from several different takes, and was one of the songs Steve Lillywhite mixed in the album's final months.
That chiming guitar is a six-note arpeggio played through a dotted-eighth delay, so each note sounds twice. Bass and drums don't enter until 1:10 — and Bono waits nearly two minutes to sing.

It was the album's third single, released August 31, 1987 — a slot originally meant for 'Red Hill Mining Town.' Its B-sides included 'Sweetest Thing,' which U2 re-recorded into a hit of its own in 1998.
Chart report: No. 13 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 4 in the UK, and No. 1 in Ireland.

The video was shot March 27, 1987 on a liquor-store roof at 7th and Main in downtown Los Angeles — a nod to the Beatles' rooftop concert. The roof was reinforced for a week beforehand, over 1,000 people gathered, and U2 played an eight-song set, doing this song four times.

The police shutdown in the video really happened — though manager Paul McGuinness later admitted the confrontation was exaggerated, as officers kept granting extensions. The audio is the studio version, and the clip won the 1989 Grammy for Best Performance Music Video.

title: Where The Streets Have No Name

description: U2's Bo Diddley-beat rocker from Rattle and Hum — the released version is the band's original Dublin demo. It became their first UK No. 1 single and won the 1989 Grammy for Best Rock Performance.

pops.text: The groove is the Bo Diddley beat, and U2 cite the Stooges' '1969' as the song's primary influence. Three minutes, one immortal rhythm.

What you're hearing is a demo. U2 first cut 'Desire' at STS Studios in Dublin, then re-recorded it at A&M in Los Angeles — tighter, said The Edge, but it 'lacked feel.' They scrapped it and released the demo.
It's track three on Rattle and Hum and was the album's lead single, released September 19, 1988. The whole song runs just 2:59.
That's Bono himself on harmonica, and the producer is Jimmy Iovine — the same man behind Tom Petty's Damn the Torpedoes.
Chart history: 'Desire' became U2's first No. 1 single in the UK and Australia, and reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100.
A Billboard first: it topped the Modern Rock Tracks and Mainstream Rock Tracks charts at the same time — the first song ever to sit at No. 1 on both simultaneously.
At the 31st Grammy Awards in 1989, it won Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal.
The video was filmed in Hollywood and directed by Richard Lowenstein and Lynn-Maree Milburn. It actually uses the 'Hollywood Remix' version, cutting in local people and images riffing on the lyrics.

Live, it debuted on the first night of the Lovetown Tour, September 21, 1989, seguing into Bob Dylan's 'All Along the Watchtower.' On the Zoo TV Tour, Bono performed it in character as Mirror Ball Man and MacPhisto.

An early studio performance appears in the 1988 Rattle and Hum film, and the song earned spots on both The Best of 1980–1990 and U218 Singles. Its B-side, 'Hallelujah Here She Comes,' has never been played in full live.

title: Desire
